Why are we needing to verify this by hand now?  is verifyMtlsUser callback not called in the resumption case?

No it's not, this is the point. Here are the flows:
1. First connection.
Client presents client certs and no session id.
Server does handshake, cert validation (self-signed, expiration, etc) and calls the callback if it's set. The callback calls verifyMtlsUser for certificates it received, and populates mtlsSession.
Server assigns session id, stores session -> certificates in the cache and returns session id to the client.

2. Subsequent connections
Client presents session id and no client certs.
Server does cache lookup using the session id and populates certs into connection object. It does NOT do re-validation, thus it does not call the callback, so verifyMtlsUser is not called and the mtlsSession is not populated.

That's the problem I'm solving here, as the mtlsSession is not populated, requests received via subsequent connections are not authenticated from the server perspective.

To solve this, I call verifyMtlsUser and populate results to mtlsSession as the callback does for the first connection, but now, I use the SSL object openssl constructed from cache using session id to retrieve certs for validation.
Done

Where I worry is that we've now split the "how do we turn a certificate into a user" path.  Just because the session is resumed doesn't mean the user is still valid.

Is there any way we can deduplicate?  If we're now no longer relying on the callback, should we just take the "normal" path at all times?

As much as possible I'm trying to keep openssl out of the public headers.  I think we can just pass boost::asio::ssl::verify_context and pull native_handle() out within the method?

No, unfortunately we cannot pass that type, as we don't get boost::asio::ssl::verify_context on the caller side (in the afterSslHandshake function). The boost::asio::ssl::verify_context object is a temp object constructed only on the Certificate validation on the handshake phase (the callback is called from this phase), and it gets destroyed after Certificate validation/handshake is completed, so it's not available later in afterSslHandshake (full SSL object is available there).

In resumption case, the subsequent requests do not pass client cert, but session ID. So, OpenSSL does not do cert validation (they are not provided, but they are already validated and cached), so it does not call the call back. Instead, it does a lookup in the session cache, and reconstructs SSL object. This object persists until the connection is destroyed. So, in the afterSslHandshake function the only source of the certs is the SSL object, we retrieve it using adaptor.native_handle(). Though, I added a workaround, not to include openssl to the header.
Done

I'm not understanding this.  The session cache persists between number of connections.  The 200 limit in bmcweb is MAX CONCURRENT connections, not total for the lifetime of the process, so technically we'd be bounded at the 20000 limit, right?

OpenSSL cleans up expired entries from the cache every on 255th new session: https://docs.openssl.org/3.6/man3/SSL_CTX_flush_sessions/#notes. So the only case all the 20K entries will be used is some sort of DoS. But to play on the safe side, I think it worth to set limit.

I'm confused why we would see a 401?  Shouldn't we just see a sessions resumption cache miss, which should silently still connect?

No. There are 3 moving parts here:
1. Boost that passes client certs in boost::asio::ssl::verify_context to BMCWeb. This happens only when client passed the certs (TLS session resumption is disable or it's the 1st connection in a session).
2. OpenSSL that constructs SSL object that contain clients certs, the object exists during connection lifetime - for the 1st connection or TLS session resumption disabled case the client certs are taken from the client request; for the TLS session resumption subsequent connections associated with existing session, it picks up the certs corresponding to the session from the cache.
3. BMCweb. It does client auth using certificates. Before this change, the only place where auth was happening had been the callback which is called only when client passes certificates - TLS session resumption disabled, or it's a 1st connection of TLS session resumption session.

So, before this change, for subsequent connections OpenSSL tried to populate certificates from the cache to SSL object, but as cache was not created, it could not, but it did not fail on this, it just did not populate certs. That's why the connection did not fail with anything like "cache miss". However, even if it could, since BMCweb did not do user cert auth except of in the callback that covers only the 1st connection, and a user is not authenticated by default, attempt to access to a "restricted" area failed with 401.


So to fix this, we need to do 2 things - enable cache, so OpenSSL would link certificates presented by a client in the 1st connection to subsequent ones; and have BMCweb to auth user not only in the callback, but after the SSL object is reconstructed. This is what this diff does.

> OpenSSL tried to populate certificates from the cache to SSL object

This is the part I'm confused about.  We didn't enable certificate caching or resumption, so how could this be true?

If this is true, yes, I agree, the rest makes sense.

I did some more digging and found my previous assumption about default cache state was wrong - I though it does not exist by default, and the code just bypasses cache lookup, so the SSL object created for resumption case does not have certificates. 
In fact the cache does exist by default, its size set to 20K, mode to SSL_SESS_CACHE_SERVER. So, for the first connection / resumption disabled a client sends certs, openssl put them to the cache and auth happened in the callback; for subsequent connections within the session, openssl populated certs from the cache, but as bmcweb did not do auth in the afterSslHandshake (the callback was not called either), despite the cert was in the SSL object, user was not authorized and server sent 401.
Done

Is there a reason you wrote this yourself rather than use constructX509?

constructX509 is not quite re-usable here:
1. It's a static and is not exposed in hpp file.
2. It generates a key+cert bundle as a string, here we need just X509, if the test reuses the function, the string will need to be parsed.
3. constructX509 generates production cert with particular extensions and properties (country, org). So constructX509 is a "give me a complete cert file" function. MtlsHandshake needs fine-grained control to set up specific test scenarios (null certs, missing extensions, etc.).

1. Is trivially fixable without rewriting code
2. Why is parsing a problem?  This is a unit test.  Functionally it will be a lot less duplicated code.
3. Can we just pass in an argument for these things?
